wine.name: Lyrarakis Plyto Psarades
wine.grapes: Plyto alone, an old white grape of Crete that the family brought back from near loss.
wine.sites: The family's Psarades vineyard near Alagni in the hills of central Crete, at about 480 metres, where Plyto and Dafni were first planted in 1992.
wine.making: The grapes are destemmed and lightly crushed, and by the house's own vintage sheets the method moves with the year: in some vintages part or all of the must spends from a few hours to two days on its skins before a cool fermentation, and in some years a share of the wine has a short spell in oak before bottling.
wine.glass: White peach, pear and quince over a chalky, faintly salty edge that recalls shellfish; rich and full in the mouth, with a long, herbal finish.
wine.ageing: Ready on release and at its liveliest in its first few years; the sources read here give it no long keeping life.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, as the house advises; no need to decant; a white wine glass of moderate size.

records.table: A Cretan grape that had almost vanished makes Lyrarakis Plyto Psarades, from the vineyard near Alagni where the family planted it in 1992. White peach and pear meet a salty, herbal edge, a natural partner for shellfish.
records.story: The winery dates from 1966, when two brothers of the Lyrarakis family founded it at Alagni, a village in the hills south of Heraklion. As Crete replanted its vineyards in the decades that followed, the island's old local grapes gave way to more productive ones, and Plyto and Dafni, two whites of central Crete, came close to being lost. They were the first grapes the family set out to research, and in 1992 it planted both in its Psarades vineyard at about 480 metres. The first wines of each grape alone followed in 1996, by the house's own account, the first time either name was printed on a label. The house tells of long years of obstacles from state agencies before the old grapes could be planted and labelled freely; that is its own telling, and it adds that those restrictions have since almost vanished. In 2010 Melissaki, a grape the family found in the foothills of Mount Psiloritis, joined them in its Gerodeti vineyard, the third old grape the house says it saved. Plyto carries the whole idea of the house: a grape nearly gone, kept alive in one family vineyard and poured again by the glass. Crete's revival of its own white grapes is in this bottle, and no other island can pour it.

wine.name: Douloufakis Dafnios Vidiano
wine.grapes: Vidiano alone, an old white grape of Crete to which the family turned in 2000.
wine.sites: The family's own vineyards on the hill slopes around Dafnes, south of Heraklion, at about 350 metres, on clay loam rich in lime, by the house's sheets.
wine.making: Made as a classic white: the juice is fermented in stainless steel tanks at about 18 degrees Celsius, and the wine sees no barrel in either fermentation or maturation before it is bottled, by the house's own sheet.
wine.glass: Peach and apricot over chamomile, jasmine and wild herbs, with a stony edge; full in the mouth, with fresh, balanced acidity and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Fresh and open on release; the house says it may be kept for up to five years.
wine.serve: 9 to 10 degrees Celsius, as the house advises for the Dafnios white; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

records.table: From the family's vineyards around Dafnes, south of Heraklion, Douloufakis Dafnios Vidiano is an old Cretan white grape fermented cool in steel and kept from oak. Peach, apricot and chamomile make it a match for Cretan greens or a plate of fish.
records.story: The family's winemaking begins in 1930, when the founder, grandfather of the family's third generation, began to make wine professionally in old premises at Dafnes, as the house tells it. His son took the winery on in 1960. Phylloxera reached Crete around 1977, by the house's account, and destroyed most of the island's vineyards; the replanting at Dafnes began in 1980 and lasted nearly a decade. The first bottled wines came in 1997: a dry red of Liatiko from the Dafnes appellation and a dry white of Sauvignon Blanc. In 2000 the founder's grandson, of the third generation, turned to Vidiano, a white grape of Crete then in danger of extinction, and the grape became the heart of the house's whites. Dafnios, the adjective of Dafnes, ties the wine to its village, and the white Dafnios is pure Vidiano made in steel. Other Cretan houses took up the grape over the same years, and Vidiano went from near loss to a white poured across the island and beyond it. The Dafnios gives the grape unoaked and unadorned, from a family that turned to it while it was still in danger.

wine.name: Oikonomoy Sitia Liatiko
wine.grapes: Liatiko, the great majority and at least four fifths by the Sitia rules, from a local clone of the plateau.
wine.sites: Vineyards around Ziros, Katsidoni and Etia on the Ziros plateau above Sitia, at about 600 to 650 metres.
wine.making: Fermented spontaneously in stainless steel, by merchants' notes, then aged for years at the estate in oak, in steel and in bottle: sixteen months in 350 litre Burgundian casks on one sheet, three years and more in barrel on a visitor's account. The estate releases a vintage only when it judges it ready, often a decade or more after the harvest.
wine.glass: Pale garnet turning brick at the rim; orange peel, sour red cherry and thyme, with fine, dry tannin and fresh acidity carried through long age.
wine.ageing: Released already mature, often a decade or more after the harvest; it is ready when poured and keeps for some years more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant gently off any sediment shortly before serving; a Burgundy glass for its perfume.

records.table: Released only when the estate judges it ready, often a decade after the harvest, Domaine Economou's Sitia Liatiko grows on the Ziros plateau in the far east of Crete. Pale and mature, with orange peel, red cherry and thyme, it suits roast lamb.
records.story: The estate stands on the Ziros plateau above Sitia, at the eastern end of Crete, among the family's vineyards. Its founder, born on Crete, studied agriculture in Milan and oenology at Alba in Piedmont, worked in cellars there and in Baden in Germany, and then at Château Margaux, before he came home in 1994 and began to make wine from the family's vines, as the accounts of the estate tell it. He built the reds on the plateau's own clone of Liatiko, a pale red grape, and treated it as a wine for long keeping, aged in oak, steel and bottle at the estate before release. The winery keeps no fixed release calendar, so its vintages reach the market when they are judged ready rather than in order: its 2004 Antigone, by one merchant's account, spent nearly eighteen years in steel, old oak and bottle before it was sold. Sitia's appellation calls for at least four fifths Liatiko in its red, with Mandilaria beside it. The estate also makes Odyssey, a white of Thrapsathiri from old vines on their own roots. Its Sitia shows how far a light Cretan red can age: a mature wine, ready the moment it is poured.

wine.name: Alexakis Vidiano
wine.grapes: Vidiano alone, the old white grape of Crete.
wine.sites: Vineyards of the Heraklion district at about 550 metres, on sandy clay rich in calcium, by the house's own account.
wine.making: After destemming, the grapes are given about eight hours of cold maceration on their skins and the free run juice is drawn off without pressing; it is then fermented in stainless steel tanks for fifteen to twenty days, never above 16 degrees Celsius, by the house's own account.
wine.glass: Peach and apricot over pear, lime zest and a grassy note, with a flinty edge and a gently bitter, peel like finish.
wine.ageing: A wine for its youth, poured within its first few years while the fruit is fresh; no source read here claims a long life for it.
wine.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: The white grape of Crete, nearly abandoned before trial wines of the 1980s revived it.

records.table: Alexakis Vidiano is Crete's revived white grape from a large Heraklion family house that buys from growers across the island. Fermented cool in steel from vineyards at about 550 metres, it shows peach, apricot and a grassy freshness that wants drinking young, beside seafood.
records.story: The house was founded in Heraklion in the 1970s, some years after two brothers had founded Lyrarakis at Alagni in 1966, by a chemical engineer and oenologist with his wife, and it has stayed a family business, run with their two sons, both oenologists, as the house tells it. It grew into what it calls the largest private winery on Crete, at Peridi Metochi on the road from Heraklion to Malades, working under contract with growers across the island and above all around Heraklion. Vidiano, by the house's own history of the grape, had been grown on Crete for centuries and was nearly abandoned until producers began small trial vinifications in the 1980s; from them the grape came back to the vineyards of Heraklion and of Rethymno. The house made Vidiano one of its leading wines, and the island's producers' association names it among the house's export wines, beside a Kotsifali with Syrah and a white of Dafni, and it sells in America under its own Alexakis name. One trade account counts the founder's sons among the young winemakers who brought the grape back from fading, beside the Douloufakis family at Dafnes, whose third generation turned to it in 2000. This is the widely found, approachable Vidiano, a first glass of the grape before the estate bottlings of Dafnes and Alagni.

wine.appellation: PGI Crete, or varietal wine of Greece by vintage
wine.grapes: Roussanne alone, the white grape of the Rhône, first planted here in 1993.
wine.sites: The family's organically farmed vineyards around Vatolakkos in the foothills of the Lefka Ori, the White Mountains, west of Chania; the first vines went in at about 350 metres.

wine.glass: Peach, apricot and honey over toast and vanilla from the oak, with a floral lift; full and rich in the mouth, with a long finish.

records.table: Near Chania, in the foothills of the White Mountains, a Rhône grape makes Manousakis Nostos Roussanne, its name the Greek for homecoming. Fermented and aged in French oak, it is full and honeyed with peach and apricot, a white for roast chicken or rich fish.
records.story: The founder's family came from Vatolakkos, a village near Chania in the west of Crete, and after years abroad he came back to make wine there, as the family tells it. In 1993 the first vines went in, farmed organically by the house's account, and they were not the island's own grapes but Roussanne, Syrah, Grenache and Mourvèdre of the Rhône, chosen on the advice of an American vine consultant. The family called the wines Nostos, the Greek for the longing to return home. In the summer of 1997, with the first harvest, it finished building its winery on the grounds of the family home, and the house tells that the surprise of that first year was how much fruit the Roussanne gave in Crete. The founder's daughter took up the winemaking in 2007, and the family later added Cretan grapes such as Romeiko, first planted at its Gouverneto site in 2018, and Assyrtiko bought from growers. The Roussanne is the white the house is known by: a Rhône grape made into a full, oak aged white on a Mediterranean island. On a Cretan list it is the counterpoint: a house that began with France rather than with the island's revival of its own grapes.

questions.q: A guest asks how Manousakis Nostos Roussanne is raised before bottling. What is the true reply?
opts: About seven months in French oak barrels
Two years in large old casks
Steel only, on its fine lees
In clay jars buried in the ground
questions.exp: It is fermented and aged in French oak barrels, about seven months by merchants' sheets, which gives its toast and vanilla; it is not a steel raised white.

questions.q: Which grapes did the Manousakis family first plant at Vatolakkos in 1993?
questions.exp: The first vines were Rhône varieties chosen on an American consultant's advice; Romeiko was first planted only in 2018, and the Assyrtiko is bought from growers.

sources.title: Insights Greece: organic boutique winery in a village of Chania

report: Searches for this record: seven of the group's 35; no fetch tried. The plan's doubt is answered: the house, its village of Vatolakkos and its Nostos range are confirmed by its own pages, the producers' association and three trade sources.

The founding year is 1993 on the house's pages and in a Wine Enthusiast profile reprinted by the association; one retailer gives 1983 and one magazine 1984, the year the house says the dream began, so founded is 1993, the planting.
The founder, his daughter and the vine consultant are living and not named; the consultant's name appears on the house's page.
The appellation differs by vintage and seller: PGI Crete on two importers' sheets, Wine of Greece or varietal wine on two others, so the field says so; a refuter with a label in hand may settle it.
The seven months in French oak is two Greek merchants' sheets; no sheet of the house was read, and lees handling was found in no source.
The plan names Romeiko as the local red the house is known for; the only Romeiko wines found were the Nostos Pink and one listing of a white Romeiko, so Romeiko appears only in the story and others.

changed: story: was born in Vatolakkos; the sources read say the family's village and a return to his Cretan roots, so now the founder's family came from Vatolakkos.
story, question: was Romeiko and Assyrtiko added later without a year; now Romeiko first planted at Gouverneto in 2018 and Assyrtiko bought from growers, by the house's pages.
story: organic farming from the start hedged as the house's account.
open: The appellation differs by vintage (PGI Crete or Wine of Greece); the field keeps both.
The seven months in French oak rests on Greek merchants' sheets; no sheet of the house was read.
